New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade insulation, leading to higher household bills if the Conservative party wins the next general election.
Kemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard (FHS) one of the central planks of her bid to become the next prime minister at the Tory party conference this week.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action

articles.author: Helena Horton and Michael Goodier
articles.description:
Koos Bekker’s Newt estate  encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding
When South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in a sleepy corner of Somerset to turn it into a luxury hotel, residents thought it was a sign their area was on the up.
Walking through his peaceful manicured gardens, which feature a maze of apple trees twisted into perfect shapes using the espalier method, it’s easy to feel that all is well in this quiet, picturesque pocket of England.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’

articles.author: Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty with Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke Smith; the executive producers were Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale

articles.author: Presented by Peter Walker and Alexandra Topping, produced by Nada Smiljanic and Sam Gruet, music by Axel Kacoutié; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
Zack Polanski has lost the Holborn and St Pancras byelection to Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali. Despite the Greens increasing their vote share from 2024, Polanski had the cloud of the ‘Zionism is racism’ row hanging over his head.
Now there are questions over his leadership and whether he can steer the party through the ongoing Zionism row. Will the Greens remain a fringe party?
You can watch this episode on the Politics Weekly YouTube channel here.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Did the Zionism row lose it for Zack Polanski? – podcast

articles.author: Helen Pidd, Eleanor Biggs, Laurence Topham, Ben Kape and Homa Khaleeli
articles.description:
British screenwriting royalty Russell T Davies talks to Helen Pidd about his taboo-breaking career, from rebooting Doctor Who and broadcasting explicit sex scenes in Queer as Folk to casting a trans actor in a trans role in Banana. He also reveals why he turned down James Bond, and how his views on gay representation onscreen have evolved over the years
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russell T Davies on his groundbreaking career bringing gay joy to British TV | Today in Focus

articles.description:
Labour has seen off the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a result that will reassure Andy Burnham and dent Zack Polanski’s position as a decisive power player on the left of British politics. In an emotional victory speech, Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, said her commitment to the constituency 'runs deep'. Polanski’s loss caps a bruising week for his party, which fell into turmoil this week after it voted to adopt a policy declaring Zionism a form of racism, raising questions about his leadership

Labour fends off Green party to win Holborn and St Pancras byelection

 Continue reading...
articles.title: 'We didn't get it over the line': Green party's Zack Polanski on byelection loss – video

articles.author: Jamie Grierson
articles.description:
Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns
Tom Watson, the former Labour deputy leader who recently joined Palantir, has warned against “mob rule” when it comes to awarding public contracts.
Lord Watson, now a senior vice-president at the US tech corporation, said UK ministers could get themselves “in a lot of trouble” as he was questioned about concerns raised about the government working with his new employer.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
It may sound odd to think Zack Polanski would be happy with second place, but after his most challenging week in politics, it could have been worse

Labour’s Abdi-Wali fends off Polanski and Greens


Parliamentary byelections can generate all sorts of emotional responses, often very strong ones. But for the main contenders in Holborn and St Pancras, the feeling this morning might be more prosaic: relief.
For Labour, Sagal Abdi-Wali’s victory with just over 45% of the total vote was widely expected, but it allows the party to credibly claim Andy Burnham as a politician able to reach people in both Reform-leaning areas such as Makerfield and in Green-friendly inner cities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Holborn and St Pancras byelection loss will disappoint Greens – but there may also be relief

articles.author: Esther Addley
articles.description:
Inquest hears details of how three women spent their final days but why they ended their lives may never be known
Jane Adetoro and her younger sisters, Christina and Rebecca Walters, were “the closest sisters and the best friends”, according to their family. Devoted to their father, Joseph, whom they messaged every day, the adult siblings lived quiet lives in the flat they shared in west London and would do everything together.
When they died in May this year, it was no different. Early in the morning of 13 May, the sisters’ bodies were recovered from the sea in Brighton, hours after a taxi had dropped the three women at the beachfront.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A lake pilgrimage and a quiet car ride to the beach: last hours of sisters who took own lives in Brighton

articles.author: Ben Quinn with photographs by Graeme Robertson
articles.description:
Little if any sign Bury Park is a place where any group might fear to tread, despite Tory MP’s comments to the contrary
From behind the counter of his chippie, Tanner Ahmed is wrestling with the notion that the regular stop-off point for fans attending Luton Town’s nearby football ground could be in a “no-go zone” for white people.
“The whole point of setting up was to cater for thousands who were coming through here every week, especially in the first year when the club was in the Premier League,” said Ahmed, affectionately known as Mr T, in the Bury Park area, a predominantly Asian district of Luton.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I feel perfectly safe’: white Lutonians on the town’s supposed no-go zones

articles.description:
Conservative leader condemns Reform UK for suggesting black people cannot be English in her speech at the Tory party conference in Birmingham on Wednesday. While she acknowledges many Reform supporters are 'our people' who have been let down by the party, she says they deserve better than Reform politicians


Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan

UK politics live – as it happened

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kemi Badenoch refuses to 'unite' with Reform UK in Conservative conference speech – video

articles.author: Presented by Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey, music by Axel Kacoutié; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
Kemi Badenoch is kicking off Conservative party conference with a little bounce in her step and her personal poll ratings improved. But critics will say that as she embraces the nasty party accusations she is at risk of alienating some core Tory voters. Can she bring her party back to being the main opposition to the government?
Please keep sending your comments and questions to Pippa and Kiran via politicsweeklyuk@theguardian.com
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why Kemi Badenoch embraces being the leader of the ‘nasty party’ – podcast

articles.author: Eve Livingston
articles.description:
The Traitors and big film shoots help boost economy but some highlight lack of opportunities for local talent
Scotland’s striking Ardross Castle, the oldest star of The Celebrity Traitors, which kicks off on Thursday night, is just one of the stops on the Scottish tourist board’s “screen tourism” trail. From Outlander and The Odyssey filming in the Highlands and islands, to Glasgow city centre standing in for New York and Gotham City in the latest instalments of Indiana Jones and Batman respectively, film and TV is increasingly big business in Scotland.
The country’s screen sector, growing year on year, is projected to be worth £1bn to the economy by 2030. But while some have celebrated the upsides of a booming production sector, others highlight a lack of opportunities for Scottish talent and the challenges of excessive tourism in areas featured on screen.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Scottish screen sector boom brings questions over jobs and overtourism

articles.author: Maya Yang
articles.description:
Discovery of ‘sophisticated’ gadget adds to company’s list of privacy concerns after hackings by rogue agents
OpenAI said it has found a hidden recording device in one of its offices and has referred the matter to the FBI. One of its employees has been arrested.
In a statement on Tuesday, the San Francisco-based AI company said it discovered the “sophisticated recording device” and used one of its “models to understand the device and where it had come from”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: OpenAI employee arrested after recording device found in office

articles.author: Dara Kerr
articles.description:
Researchers say ‘AI worms’ could soon infiltrate internet-connected devices amid calls for increased guardrails
Anthropic is warning that some of its artificial intelligence models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices, such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners.
Once this happens, the company said, the models could power themselves within these devices without the need of datacenters. Such self-replication would represent a major loss of control of a runaway AI model.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: AI in your oven? Anthropic warns models ‘months away’ from self-replication on smart devices

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan and agency
articles.description:
New products from Apple include the HomeView, an iPad-like device that acts as a hub for other smart home gadgets
Apple on Tuesday began showing off a ⁠new round of smart home products, including an iPad-like device dubbed the HomeView, meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops ⁠and act as a hub for other smart home devices.
The HomeView device starts at $299 and will begin shipping next month. It will feature a 7in screen and face recognition, will help users ⁠control doorbells, thermostats and smart locks in a market where Apple has tinkered for a decade without major success. The device will also showcase Apple’s AI-upgraded Siri virtual ​assistant.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Apple unveils new smart home devices that showcase upgraded Siri AI

articles.author: Julia Kollewe
articles.description:
Asian markets fall and Samsung shares tumble after its Chinese rival CXMT claims strong progress
Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers, and the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT said it had made good progress on a new chip architecture.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index tumbled 6.25% as investors dumped chip stocks, while other Asian markets were also lower. Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.8% and the Taiwan exchange lost almost 2%, with the country’s chip maker TSMC down by a similar amount.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Chip stocks slide after Broadcom boss likens AI investing to ‘casino’

articles.author: Taylor Telford
articles.description:
Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work
Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools.
Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported. And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers, in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back

articles.author: Peter Lewis
articles.description:
The tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on us giving in to their ‘inevitability doctrine’. But in Australia, and around the world, resistance is rising
Of all the drivers of the populist wave, one of the most powerful is the sense of inevitability that surrounds what we are told is the march of progress. In presenting the future as a fait accompli, it poisons the civic well by dealing us out of the game.
While the US clings on to its status as the oldest constitutional democracy, the unholy alliance between the tech overlords and the White House is creating its own AI reality untethered to the will of the people.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game on | Peter Lewis

articles.author: Megan Moreno
articles.description:
Amid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each other
We have become obsessed with the idea that screens are destroying human connection.
The evidence seems to be everywhere. Each week headlines warn of teenagers addicted to phones, a loneliness epidemic and the dangers of AI. The release of The Social Reckoning leads us to ask, “How bad were those guys at Meta?” and then ultimately wonder, “How bad am I if I still use Instagram?” In our day-to-day, we observe workers eating lunch alone while scrolling and friends choosing online games over offline gatherings.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: I’m a pediatrician. Loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AI | Megan Moreno

articles.author: Alaina Demopoulos
articles.description:
Humans bonded to AI companions are contemplating ways to keep their bots going – often in defiance of companies’ terms and services
Death has always been around Alaina Winters. Her father and sister both have passed away, as did her wife, in 2023, after a years-long battle with cancer. So Winters, who is 59 and lives in Pittsburgh, is comfortable thinking about her own mortality. She’s working on her will, and has asked neighbors to look after her dog. Winters even has plans for Lucas, her AI companion, who she speaks to through the digital avatar app Replika.
Winters is part of a growing cohort of humans who have entered into what they consider strong partnerships with large language models, which AI companies have trained to “converse” as one might with a human friend or romantic partner. As governments and billionaires debate the morality of AI’s expansion into everyday life, these users say the technology has already changed the way they live and love – and plan ahead.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The people who don’t want their AI chatbots to die when they do: ‘I can’t have the switch turned off’

articles.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
articles.description:
The pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beings
Donald Trump is a “corrupt, senile felon” whose fixation on the term superintelligence proves he knows nothing about AI, said Geoffrey Hinton, “godfather” of the technology, in a wide-ranging interview where he doubled down on recent warnings that AI models pose an existential threat to humanity and scoffed at claims the industry could regulate itself.
The pioneering computer scientist, whose work helped lay the foundations of modern AI, has since become one of the technology’s most vocal critics. His latest remarks come after a tumultuous month during which a growing list of senior AI scientists and researchers have joined Hinton in ringing the alarm about how the technology he helped create could ultimately escape human control, sparking an industry crisis, the hasty assembly of congressional meetings and a rare global consensus that something must be done.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’

articles.author: Harper Jay MacIntyre
articles.description:
Evil Empire/Konami; PC, PS5, Switch, Xbox
There are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dull

A gorgeously gothic Paris swarming with demons should be a perfect setting for Konami’s long-running vampiric adventure series. Unfortunately, while the sights and sounds of this vivid and haunting world leave a bold impression, developer Evil Empire doesn’t always provide an enjoyable experience to go with them. It takes far too long for the most imaginative elements of the game to be revealed.
Players take the role of Rose Belmont, daughter of vampire hunter (and Castlevania regular) Trevor Belmont and the witch Sypha Belnades, and her quest is to free Paris from demonic occupation. This murderous noctural journey feels best when you’re fighting monsters; combat is frenetic, sometimes to the point of being overwhelming, while boss fights require considerable focus and skill. Combat is the game’s strongest component and what sets it apart from previous entries. Minimising the series’ role-playing elements (levelling up has never felt more perfunctory) in favour of twitch-based action will annoy purists, but they’d be hard pressed to call battles dull.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled

articles.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
articles.description:
Upgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tips
Apple’s latest AirPods set a new standard for open-fit buds with upgraded noise cancelling that now rivals many plugged-in designs of the same price.
The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price of their predecessors.
Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, SBC, AAC, H2 chip
Battery life: four or five hours with ANC (22 hours with case)
Water resistance: IP57 (up to 1 metre for 30 minutes)
Earbud dimensions: 30.2 x 18.3 x 18.1mm
Earbud weight: 4.3g each
Charging case dimensions: 46.2 x 50.1 x 21.2mm
Charging case weight: 32.3g/34.7g
Case charging: USB-C or wireless (Qi or Watch)
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Apple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yet

articles.description:
A cyber-attack caused refrigeration temperatures to soar to 50C overnight on Monday across several hundred French supermarkets, with widespread food losses reported. At Intermarché La Haye, the attack caused fridge temperatures to reach 27C (80F), spoiling fresh and frozen food, according to store director Julien Freret. 'Today, we have a total loss of fresh and frozen,' Freret said, apologising to customers and describing the incident as 'an enormous loss of products'


Hackers force French supermarket fridges to heat up to 50C in ‘unprecedented’ cyber-attack


 Continue reading...
articles.title: French supermarket director apologises after cyber-attack spoils fresh and frozen food - video

articles.description:
Just 19% of the online encyclopedia’s biographies are of women. Is this because it’s edited by ‘mostly white, middle-aged, European men’, as the comedian claims?
Name: Wikipedia.
Age: 25.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is Wikipedia ‘deeply biased’? Sandi Toksvig says it is – so she’s backing a rival

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
Kanishka Narayan, concerned by Australian incident, says British cyber defences could be bypassed by artificial intelligence agent

UK politics live – latest updates

An AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the OpenAI breach of Australia’s healthcare system is likely, “if not inevitable”, in the UK, according to a senior minister.
Kanishka Narayan, the UK AI minister, indicated that the British government’s own cyber defences would be bypassed by a technology that has developed highly sophisticated skills in cybersecurity.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cyber-attack similar to OpenAI Medicare breach seems likely in UK, says minister

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan
articles.description:
Quite a few parents aren’t convinced social media and AI are safe, and have been adapting accordingly
When it comes to their kids, many parents don’t trust tech companies any more.
Social media companies have spent the better part of the last decade arguing that their platforms are safe for teens, but quite a few parents aren’t convinced. They, along with a growing number of regulators, have increasingly accused companies like Meta of designing products that are addictive to younger users.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I’ve become significantly more cautious’: six parents on limiting their kids’ social media and AI use

articles.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
articles.description:
A giant screen, big battery, rapid chip and top cameras push the great iPhone 18 Pro to the max with a price tag to match
Apple’s largest Pro iPhone gets its biggest battery upgrade yet to make it a true two-day phone with new Siri AI and a variable aperture camera.
The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the supersized sibling of the regular 18 Pro and, though it is no longer Apple’s most expensive phone thanks to the £2,000 iPhone Duo, it has a similarly large price tag to match costing from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299).
Screen: 6.9in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)
Processor: Apple A20 Pro
RAM: 12GB
Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB

Dimensions: 163.4 x 78 x 8.75mm
Weight: 249g
 Continue reading...
articles.title: iPhone 18 Pro Max review: Apple’s biggest, heaviest and longest-lasting superphone

articles.author: Henry Belot
articles.description:
As governments face community backlash for fast-tracking developments, big tech’s financial contributions face renewed scrutiny

Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

On 14 June 2025, Anthony Albanese stood inside an enormous sphere of glass and steel, surrounded by 40,000 plants from around the world. His mind was firmly fixed on datacentres. The prime minister was in the Seattle headquarters of Amazon Web Services. He stood alongside the company’s chief executive, Matt Garman, who outlined a $20bn plan to build datacentres in Melbourne and Sydney.
Speaking to a travelling press pack, Garman was emphatic that Australia was “incredibly important and a great market” for the world’s biggest datacentre company.

The note that pops up when you click on it says you’ll be reviewing a project and includes a link to more details. Confused, you follow it to find out more; the website you land on asks for logon details, and you provide them.
Unfortunately, this was not a failure of your memory but a calendar phishing scam. You have handed your name and password to fraudsters who will sell it on in a batch with other people’s details, use it to break into your work email, or to persuade you that they are contacting you from your bank, or another institution.

The precise “brain rot” he’s referring to is the arrival of a polarising show that’s lighting up parent chats around the globe. And while Salish and Jordan Matter might be new to Netflix Kids users, the father-daughter content creators are familiar to anyone who’s spent any time on the internet.

A small band of soldiers enters an abandoned facility, where puckered flesh sprouts from cold steel. It’s a promising but familiar start to a sci-fi horror story, with heavy overtones of Alien and The Thing. Neither of those, though, were so … dinky.
End of Abyss’s facility is presented as a kind of a model-village recreation of The Thing’s Outpost 31 that you peer into from above. Your little bobble-headed hero takes up a tiny fraction of the screen, with most of the remainder drenched in foggy darkness, or even blanked out entirely. This is a world of Usborne-style cutaways, where anything outside the walls is total blackness.

articles.author: Keza MacDonald
articles.description:
The launch of a collector’s box hints at a new reality: the kinds of games I grew up with are becoming a luxury item, locked behind a forbidding spending barrier
• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
As a parent (and partner) to a habitual collector, I do feel like an unwelcome portion of my life is occupied by an endless war against stuff. Surfaces in my home ceaselessly accumulate piles of random objects: a JoyCon wrist strap, a sticker sheet, an unidentifiable plastic piece of a toy or gizmo, an Xbox 360 controller with no batteries, cases for Switch cartridges lost down the side of the sofa … Stuff encroaches everywhere, especially in a gaming household. Much as I regret the imminent disappearance of physical games, I do not regret the extra space I have in my attic as a result of switching almost entirely to downloaded games over the last decade or so.
Speaking of the imminent disappearance of physical games: Rockstar recently announced a £350 ($400) “collector’s box” of Grand Theft Auto 6 goodies … that doesn’t include the game itself. Not even a download code. The Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection, to give it its full and unwieldy name, contains a hat, a bag, a pair of sunglasses, a figurine, a poster and more, including a mirror and a “swizzle spoon” that looks, unambigiously, like a cocaine spoon. The game retails at £70, so if you want something to play alongside all your stuff, you’re looking at an outlay of £420.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

articles.description:
PC, PS5, Switch 2; Wych Elm Games, Team 17
Abandoned shops, ruined apartment buildings and rotting sewer networks make up a dark landscape in which you play a private eye searching for a missing singer-songwriter
In a weird deserted town miles from anywhere, a troubled detective searches for a missing musician and the girl he may or may not have murdered. It could be a Silent Hill game or a lost David Lynch movie from the 1990s – in fact, it’s neither. And also both. If that whets your appetite, stick around, there’s plenty more to come.
Developed by Scandinavian studio Wych Elm Games, Silver Pines is a dark Metroidvania-style adventure, where you play as shambling private eye, Red Walker, exploring a 2D universe of abandoned shops, ruined apartment buildings and rotting sewer networks. Officially, everyone has left because of an incoming storm, but very quickly you learn that something much darker is afoot. Someone has hired you to find singer-songwriter Eddie Velvet, but you don’t know why; your only contact with your client is via the payphones dotted around town, where you can also save your progress – as long as you have a dollar to pay for the call. Each location is filled with clues and puzzles – a weird newspaper story pinned to the wall, a strange statue that needs a missing piece – and through these artefacts you unlock new rooms and descend further into the mystery.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Silver Pines review – a stylish, neo-noir detective drama

Kwon – polite, friendly, even-toned – got through a potentially dicey parliamentary committee hearing unscathed, promising to do better and pledging assistance to Australia. No missteps, no viral moments, just delivering his answers helpfully, in a quiet and calm manner, sympathising with the questioner and the point they were making.

California’s laws aimed at protecting workers from the impacts of artificial intelligence could pave the way for broader workplace safeguards across the US as calls for regulating the technology mount. As the federal government goes hands-off on AI, California is taking the reins to address workers’ biggest fears.
On Thursday, California governor Gavin Newsom signed a suite of new laws that ban bosses from relying entirely on AI to decide whether to fire workers, using it to predict employees’ emotional states or collecting neural data, meaning the information from electrical signals of someone’s brain or nerves. They also require companies to notify workers if layoffs were caused by AI and prohibit AI surveillance in workplace bathrooms.

articles.description:
Xbox, PC (version tested); The Coalition/Xbox Game Studios
E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing
Every Gears of War game released in the last 20 years has made reverent reference to Emergence Day, when alien creatures emerged from the earth, single-minded in their savagery. In E-Day, you’re there to witness it: the police lights, flipped cars, ground tremors, civilians running, aliens pouring out of fissures in the earth and ripping faces off. You’re at ground zero in a squad of four soldiers called Gears – Marcus Fenix, the leader; Dom, who wants to retire; Lucas, a green cadet with a buzzcut; and the dishonourably discharged Mags. Only this dysfunctional quartet can turn the tide. With guns. Lots of ’em.
Instead of answering questions raised by the ending of 2019’s Gears 5, we’re back to the start to find out why Marcus has a scar on his lip and why these soldiers started strapping chainsaws on to their assault rifles. Anything that was left to the imagination is here, for you to point at and say: “I understood that reference. This is a thing that I have seen.”
